text:
Let the Parking Lot Go

Every city that wants cheaper housing, cleaner air and a stronger local economy should start with a quiet line in its zoning code. It is the minimum parking requirement. Scrap it. Not because cars are villains, but because a rule that forces everyone to build parking, whether or not they need it, is a hidden tax on almost everything a city says it wants.

Consider how the rule works. A planner in the 1960s or 70s looked at a manual of suburban parking counts and wrote a number into the code. Two spaces per apartment. One space per 250 square feet of retail. One space for every three seats in a restaurant. The numbers were often drawn from a handful of surveys at suburban sites with free parking and little transit. They were then copied from town to town until they looked like natural law. Nobody ever proved that a downtown bakery needs eleven spaces. The code simply said so.

The cost of those spaces is real, and it lands on people who never park in them. A surface space takes roughly three hundred square feet once you count the aisles. A space in a structure can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and underground spaces cost far more. That money does not vanish. Developers pass it into rents and sale prices, and tenants who own no car pay for the concrete anyway. Researchers who study housing costs have found that mandated parking can raise the price of an apartment by a meaningful share. In a city short of homes, that is a policy choice to make homes scarcer.

It also kills projects before they begin. A small lot that could hold eight apartments may only hold four once the code demands a space for each. A historic main street building that wants to become a cafe or a clinic may be blocked because there is no room to add a lot behind it. Old neighborhoods built before the requirements could never be legally built today. The charm people love about them is, in many cases, illegal to reproduce.

Then there is the land itself. In many American downtowns, the area given over to parking rivals the area given over to everything else. Those lots pay little in property tax compared with buildings on the same ground. A city that spends its most valuable acreage on empty asphalt is starving its own budget. Studies of downtown parcels have repeatedly shown that a block with shops and homes generates far more tax revenue per acre than a block of surface lots.

The usual objection is that without requirements, developers will build no parking and neighborhoods will be choked with cars hunting for spaces. This gets the logic backwards. Removing a minimum does not impose a maximum. It lets the builder decide. Developers who believe tenants want parking will build it, because they want to fill their buildings. Lenders often ask for it too. What changes is that the number comes from the market and the site rather than from a formula nobody can defend. A building near a train station might provide fewer spaces. A building on a highway edge might provide plenty. Both outcomes are better than one number imposed on every lot.

Cities that have tried this are instructive. Buffalo repealed its citywide minimums in 2017, and the sky did not fall. Many projects there still included parking, but others became possible that were not before. Minneapolis, Anchorage, Austin and a growing list of cities have followed with full or partial repeals, and some states have moved to restrict the rule too. The early evidence shows more housing, more variety in building types, and no wave of parking chaos.

Street congestion for spaces is a real concern, but it has a better remedy than forcing private builders to overbuild. Charge a fair price for curb space. Cities that price on-street parking by demand, as San Francisco and others have tested, keep a few spaces open on every block and cut the circling that clogs traffic. Residential permit districts can protect neighbors from spillover. Revenue from meters can pay for sidewalks and lighting in the districts that earn it. These tools manage scarcity directly. A minimum requirement merely hides the cost and spreads it onto everyone.

There is a fairness argument as well. Roughly one in ten households in many cities owns no car at all, and the share is far higher among low-income renters, older residents and people with disabilities who cannot drive. A code that bundles parking into every unit makes the poorest households subsidize the storage of other people's vehicles. Unbundling parking, so that those who want a space pay for it and those who do not are spared, is one of the plainest ways to bring housing costs down without spending a public dollar.

None of this means a car-free future arrives overnight. Most people in most American cities still drive, and they will keep driving. Good. Nothing in repeal stops them. What repeal stops is the assumption that a planner's spreadsheet knows better than a landlord, a shopkeeper and a neighbor about how much parking a given building should have.

A city that cares about affordability, tax health, walkable streets and small business should treat the minimum as the policy failure it is. Strike it from the code. Let builders count their own customers. Let the parking lot go, and let the land beneath it do some work.
